\begin{abstract}
Two joint policies can prescribe identical actions on observed inputs, yet only
one may satisfy an institution's rule for execution.  When the rule concerns
responses at unobserved inputs, an overseer cannot decide from the current
actions alone.  We develop a categorical logic of agency that specifies the
required evidence and the causal interaction that supplies it.

Owner-indexed complete-policy families parameterize receptive courteous
true-concurrent strategies.  Restricted Yoneda, Day convolution and a
dependent linear--nonlinear model make these agents first-class linear
objects, preserving ownerwise control under sequential and parallel
composition. Owned presentations admit coherent compact duals and
owner-preserving feedback, with a compact closed quotient. Finite causal
protocols also determine multiplayer games
whose players are these owners, with complete-policy strategy bijections
and exact strategic adequacy. Completed execution witnesses retain outcomes and additive
charges, and the calculus constructs legal deviations, knowledge, equilibrium,
institutional action and continuing policies.

We also identify precise local-to-global properties of these constructions.
A causal Grothendieck site makes secured matching histories a sheaf: compatible
local witnesses glue uniquely, reconstructing the secured interaction before
hiding.  Owner-local legal-policy views need not glue to an institutionally
permitted profile; we characterize this obstruction and prove its exact
transport under delegation and its effect on equilibrium.  Persistent-policy
witness sheaves and observation-anchored completed records give source-fixed
lifts of strategic and epistemic alternatives and preserve the designated
modal tests. On finite economic instances, a sheaf of local potentials
gives an exact obstruction to integrating unilateral gains and a sharp
approximate-equilibrium bound. A decision-incidence sheaf identifies an
affine information obstruction whose removal improves equilibrium welfare
in a fully evaluated disclosure game. Interaction arrays separately give
a complete finite certificate for failure of robust coalitional solvability.
These results use the existing true-concurrent semantics,
without adding probabilistic or computational structure.  The calculus remains
sound, with first-layer equational completeness for its designated models and
finite behavioural characterization in the fixed concurrent semantics.
\end{abstract}

\section*{Introduction}\label{sec:paper-introduction}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Introduction}

Consider two agents that each observe a private bit and submit a decision to an
authorization checker. Both agents submit an affirmative decision on the current
input. In one pair of policies, the first agent would also act on another input for
which the second would decline to act. In another pair, both would decline to act on
that input. The institution permits only the second pair in this comparison. A
checker that receives only the decisions made now sees the same evidence in both
cases. In the finite protocol constructed below, the checker receives two additional
entries from the complete policies. It can then distinguish the cases and issue the
token required by the executor (Section~\ref{sec:agt-running-example}).

For AI alignment, this is a question about the design of oversight. A rule can refer
to counterfactual behaviour. To implement that rule, a designer must identify
evidence that distinguishes permitted from prohibited cases and a way to supply it
to the checker. The example gives the checker explicit access to two entries of a
finite policy. Applying the argument to a learned policy would require an account of
how the corresponding evidence is obtained. For cybernetics, the same example poses
a question about control under partial observation. The two decisions can occur
independently. The checker must wait for the information on which its verdict
depends, and the executor must wait for the checker's token. Which of these
dependencies survive when the whole arrangement is represented as a single
component?

Strategic games describe an owner's complete contingent choices. True-concurrent
strategies describe execution through causal prerequisites, conflict, and
independent events. We connect the two by representing each complete policy as a
parameter of a concurrent interaction. An owner can occupy several decision
positions. Changing that owner's policy can therefore change several responses at
once, including responses at positions the current execution never reaches. This is
the unit of comparison in the strategic analysis.

The owners are also players in a game semantics constructed from these
interfaces. For an arbitrary owned presentation, each owner's complete
policy is a state of its own linear policy interface; joint application
recovers the original concurrent realization
(\cref{thm:egt-mediated-multiplayer}). For a finite causal decision
protocol, we additionally construct an owner-labelled event structure of
partial plays, identify complete player strategies with the original
policies, and prove that interaction compiles to the given protocol.
Legal deviations and the retained comparison and observation tests agree
under this correspondence
(\cref{thm:egt-multiplayer-realization}). Complete response families
retain off-path choices that a single realized history can forget.
The owned bicategory has coherent compact duals and an owner-preserving
trace (\cref{thm:egt-owned-compact,thm:egt-owned-trace}). Its generated
decision fragment contains the same compact wiring; the finite acyclic
protocols provide its explicitly total forward implementations.

Four theorems develop the connection for pure policies and qualitative information.
Theorem~A gives the representation and its composition law. Theorem~B identifies the
alternatives available to an owner and evaluates them on the supplied preference and
institutional data. A completed execution records both an outcome and a charge. This
allows a budget to restrict execution and an owner to price the executions that
remain. Theorem~C constructs the protocols that deliver observations and the
continuations available after a history. Theorem~D identifies which data the
representation recovers and which tests remain valid after abstraction.

\begin{maintheorem}[Concurrent agents and compositional representation]
\label{main:A}
Receptive courteous strategies on polarized event structures form a compact
closed category $\mathcal C$ under secured interaction and hiding.
Its restricted Yoneda completion $\mathcal V$ is symmetric monoidal closed
and supports the indexed dependent linear--nonlinear structure.  For every
finite owner list $N$, ordinary complete-policy family
$\vec\Sigma=(\Sigma_i)_{i\in N}$ and original arenas $A,B$,
there is a natural bijection
\[
\mathcal V\bigl(I,[\mathsf{Lin}(\prod_i\Sigma_i)\otimes yA,yB]\bigr)
\cong\mathbf{Set}(\prod_i\Sigma_i,\mathcal C(A,B)).
\]
Under the displayed ownership signature, this representation preserves
sequential and parallel composition, ownerwise reparametrizations, and
the realization-preserving $2$-cells of the owned-open-arena bicategory.
This bicategory has coherent compact object duals; its quotient by
invertible $2$-cells is compact closed. Transposition and trace preserve
the ownerwise complete-policy families.
Each owner's complete policies are canonically the states of its own
linear policy interface, and joint application recovers the given
concurrent realization.
For an exhibited secured synchronization, the causally saturated site carries
a sheaf of matching histories; its global sections reconstruct the original
secured pullback, compatibly with parallel interaction.
\end{maintheorem}

To represent a complete policy inside an interaction, Theorem~A uses the operational
category, its Day completion, and the dependent model of
\cref{thm:egt-base,thm:egt-day-preservation,thm:egt-dependent-model}. The agent
abstraction in
\cref{agt-thm-agent-dependent-product,agt-thm-representation,agt-thm-owned-equivalence}
recovers the owner-indexed family from its internal representation. This is why a
subsequent change of policy can still be attributed to its owner.
The compact object duals and owner-preserving trace are constructed in
\cref{thm:egt-owned-compact,thm:egt-owned-trace}.

\begin{maintheorem}[Controlled, situated, and institutional agency]
\label{main:B}
Owner-coordinate projections determine compositional coalition
counterfactuals.  Owner regrouping and associative delegation preserve the
realized concurrent interaction and admit exact deviation comparisons on
the implemented policy image.  Predicate feedback along realization
constructs canonical selection, best response, and equilibrium.
Observation quotients construct admissible policy descent and knowledge;
dependent universal images construct observation-uniform legal policies.
Witnessed record-changing institutions form a symmetric monoidal bicategory,
and their dependent sums and products determine proof-relevant dynamic
modalities compatible with sequential execution.
Owner evaluation of measured records descends to profile utility exactly
when it equalizes the completed-witness kernel pair. Pullback of these
values to controlled deviations gives the cost-sensitive equilibrium test.
For owner-scope covers, legal-policy descent is exact precisely when the
specified local inspections recover the legal domain.  Its failure is
preserved under delegation onto the implemented image and can alter
legal best responses and equilibrium.
\end{maintheorem}

To test a proposed intervention, first fix the policies of everyone outside the
controlling group. Then compare the executions obtained as the group varies its own
policy. Theorem~B justifies this order of operations for regrouping, delegation, and
institutional restrictions. The component comparisons appear in
\cref{thm:egt-counterfactual,thm:egt-owner-regrouping,thm:egt-delegation-substitution,thm:cgt-coplay,agt-thm-uniform,agt-thm-institutions,agt-thm-dynamics}.
They also allow a change to be permitted even when every owner ranks it below the
reference choice.

\begin{maintheorem}[Communication, epistemic change, and continuation]
\label{main:C}
Finite owned causal decision protocols and finite binary sessions admit
true-concurrent realizations preserving complete off-path policies.
For finite causal decision protocols, the owners are the players of a
multiplayer event-structure semantics: complete strategies are canonically
their policy spaces, interaction compiles to the original realization,
and legal deviations and the designated strategic and epistemic tests
are preserved.
Their residual operations satisfy subject reduction, and secured interaction
is adequate for the completed communication witnesses.  Actual delivery
records determine epistemic action-event quotients.  For complete truthful
message policies, evaluation into the truthful public-message model is a
split surjection with the designated strategic and epistemic lifting
properties.  At the completed delivery boundary, collective disclosure
transports distributed knowledge to the stated common-knowledge and
announcement-ability predicates.  Complete local policies generate their
residual controllers, with the constructed criterion for finite-state
implementation; witnessed residual transitions support temporal fixed-point
agency and exact visible refinement.
On finite public game trees with the displayed round meter, backward
decomposition computes each child equilibrium at its inherited charge.
For exhibited finite secured protocols, persistent-policy witness sheaves
and anchored completed observation records admit exact sourcewise lifting
and modal transport of the designated epistemic and strategic alternatives.
\end{maintheorem}

Theorem~C identifies the boundary at which a delivered message can stand in for the
policy that produced it. The protocols in
\cref{thm:egt-causal-protocol,agt-thm-session,agt-lem-session-input-residual,agt-thm-message-comparison}
exhibit actual delivery and retain the responses prescribed elsewhere.
The player-strategy and interaction comparisons of
\cref{thm:egt-multiplayer-realization} identify the finite causal protocols
as multiplayer games with the same complete policies and legal alternatives.
The comparisons in \cref{agt-thm-pooling,agt-thm-disclosure} identify the information
recipients gain at that boundary. Section~\ref{sec:paper-12} asks what the agents
can still do after the exchange.

\begin{maintheorem}[Soundness, recovery, and finite behavioural completeness]
\label{main:D}
The ordinary, linear, displayed-agent, and contextual judgments of the
agency calculus are sound in the completed true-concurrent semantics.
The owner-indexed and enriched situated presentations are recovered by the
explicit reconstruction maps, while reductions relative to designated
tests retain their exhibited alternative-lifting properties.
Retaining the measured record recovers both its charge and outcome;
retaining the evaluated continuation tests preserves the corresponding
subgame-perfect predicates.

The first-layer equational calculus is complete for its class of split
indexed linear--nonlinear models by the syntactic classifying model.
In the fixed concurrent completion, original arenas separate open agent
morphisms. On image-finite retained frames, the exact bisimulation
quotient identifies precisely the states satisfying the same designated
Boolean modal tests; on finite frames, characteristic formulas define
all bisimulation-invariant predicates. Explicit finite causal-agent
interpretations have decidable semantic equality.  The structured local
witness presentations recover their completed secured histories and
retained-image modal predicates by global sections and source-fixed lifts.
\end{maintheorem}

Theorem~D answers two questions about using the calculus. Section~\ref{sec:paper-14}
identifies the displayed data that can be reconstructed and the tests that
distinguish behaviours in the fixed concurrent semantics.
Appendix~\ref{app:metatheory} proves soundness and characterizes equational
derivability by validity across the designated class of models.

The proof of each operational, strategic, or epistemic comparison follows its
statement in Parts~I--V. For the rules of the calculus, see
Appendix~\ref{app:rules}. For their soundness, reconstruction, and equational

survive passage to this semantics.

\paragraph{Finite economic obstructions.}
Three further constructions use the policy and evaluation interfaces of
Theorem~B. The decision-incidence sheaf has exactly the decentralized
joint policies as global sections; in its affine fragment a first
cohomology class is the complete implementation obstruction
(\cref{thm:egt-decision-sections,thm:egt-affine-obstruction}).
Section~\ref{sec:egt-disclosure-obstruction} calculates every equilibrium
of a binary team task before and after one-bit disclosure and evaluates
the resulting welfare improvement and fee threshold.
On the legal-deviation graph, the sheaf of local potential primitives
integrates unilateral gains exactly when its torsor class vanishes;
cycle means compute the best uniform integration error and certify an
approximate equilibrium
(\cref{thm:egt-potential-obstruction,thm:egt-cycle-mean-approximation}).
Common and own-policy charges preserve this obstruction, and whole-owner
delegation preserves and reflects it on implemented policies.
Finally, \cref{thm:egt-robust-coalitional-solvability} constructs
destabilizing integer preferences exactly when a finite blocking-selection
certificate exists. This coalitional criterion uses interaction sheaves
in their specified sense, distinguished from ordinary sheaf cohomology
in \cref{rem:egt-interaction-sheaf-distinction}.

\paragraph{Three semantic levels.}
The model has three levels. Ordinary policies and their dependent families live in
$\mathbf{Set}$. Linear interfaces, interpreted as presheaves over the concurrent strategy
category, describe the resources an execution uses. Assertions express properties of
states and execution witnesses. At the first level one can consider several policies
for a single device. Running several copies of that device would require the
corresponding resources at the second level. At the third level one can assert that
authorization occurred and, when the witness is retained, identify the event that
establishes the assertion. Causal patches of synchronization witnesses
and owner scopes of complete policies supply two local presentations.
Decision incidences and legal-deviation graphs additionally retain the
overlaps used by the finite economic obstructions. Their gluing and
comparison theorems concern the exhibited semantics and introduce no
additional type constructors.

\paragraph{What the operational semantics determines.}
Execution determines the enabled moves, their causes, the signals carried by the
wires, and the residual process. The model specifies who may change a policy and how
an owner compares outcomes. A permission rule likewise enters as institutional data.
Once a protocol implements that rule, its execution can establish that the required
event occurred. This distinction matters whenever an external observer uses the
event as evidence of authorization.

\paragraph{A running finite instance.}
The recurring example has two owners and a private bit for each: its world
carrier is $W=2\times2$, with observations $o_1(x,y)=x$ and
$o_2(x,y)=y$. At separate decision nodes owner $1$ applies
$\pi_1:2\to2$ to $x$ and owner $2$ applies $\pi_2:2\to2$ to $y$.
Thus $\Sigma_1=2^2$, $\Sigma_2=2^2$, and the complete profile carrier
has $16$ elements, including all off-path responses. The operational
realization is the tensor of the two response strategies, with their
specified private inputs. An institutional rule can couple the policies:
we use the concrete legal domain
\[
 L=\{(\pi_1,\pi_2):\pi_1(1)\leq\pi_2(1)\}\hookrightarrow
 \Sigma_1\times\Sigma_2,
\]
which has $12$ elements, using the usual order on $2=\{0,1\}$. To compare choices
at a given world, start with the exact rational payoffs $u_1(a,b)=2ab-a$ and $u_2(a,b)=2ab-b$,
where $a=\pi_1(x)$ and $b=\pi_2(y)$. A collector later delivers $(x,y)$ to the agents. A
separate checker enforces the permission rule for final execution.
Its owner-local policy images jointly contain all $16$ profiles, although
only $12$ are legal.  Secured collection of the off-path policy entries
provides the missing joint inspection evidence.  The calculations
in \cref{sec:agt-running-institution,sec:agt-running-example} show which deviations
are profitable, which facts become common knowledge, and what evidence the executor
receives.

\paragraph{Route through the paper.}
Parts~I and II follow a policy from its representation as a concurrent strategy to
the comparison of deviations under composition. Parts~III and IV follow a signal
from a private observation through a communication protocol to a decision another
owner can make with it. Part~V asks what remains possible after a history and how
much of that history a controller or an abstraction must retain.
Appendix~\ref{app:rules} gives the inference rules. Appendix~\ref{app:metatheory}
gives the reconstruction, soundness, and equational-completeness proofs.

\subsection*{Relation to the literature}

Two questions organize the comparison with earlier work. How does a process acquire
an owner whose control remains identifiable under composition? Which observations
and strategic alternatives survive a change of representation? On the first
question, the action calculi of Barber, Gardner, Hasegawa, and Plotkin connect
interaction to linear logic \citep{agt-BarberEtAl}, and resource-sensitive agency
logics connect action modalities to resources \citep{agt-PorelloTroquard}. Here the
agent itself is a typed resource. Passing it to another process must preserve the
designated ownership of its policy.

Parameterized open games distinguish policy coordinates from their evaluation
\citep{CapucciEtAl2022Agency}. Categorical cybernetics relates this distinction to
selection and the backward transport of comparisons
\citep{CapucciEtAl2022Cybernetics}. Cartesian frames describe the division of
control between agent and environment \citep{GarrabrantEtAl2021CartesianFrames}.
Section~\ref{sec:paper-4} recovers that division on unrestricted policy products and
computes the available choices when a permission rule couples the two sides. The
present construction also assigns each profile a concurrent execution, so one can
ask how an observation reaches its recipient. Session calculi relate channel
interaction to cut \citep{agt-CairesEtAl}. Our finite sessions retain the complete
endpoint policies and the matched events that witness delivery.

Multiplayer game semantics also gives an operational interpretation to the
owners themselves. \citet{Abramsky2007MultiAgent} develops a compositional
semantics of partial information using agent-labelled structures,
closure-operator strategies, and least common fixed points. Partial-order
Boolean games and finite-action partial order games assign collections of
decision nodes to players and specify responses to available predecessor
information \citep{BradfieldEtAl2016PartialOrder,ZahoranskyEtAl2022PartialOrder}.
The construction in Section~\ref{sec:egt-multiplayer-semantics} identifies
these complete response families with the existing owner policies and
compares their interaction with the concurrent implementation. Access-level
restrictions in \citet{ClairambaultEtAl2013Imperfect} explain the need to
retain the information discipline; non-zero-sum event-structure games in
\citet{GutierrezWooldridge2014Equilibria} provide a related equilibrium
semantics. The exact comparisons here use the displayed observation
quotients, legal domains, and whole-owner deviations. The distinction
between economic players and the operational environment also appears in
\citet{Hedges2020}.

For the second question, epistemic actions as resources
\citep{agt-BaltagCoeckeSadrzadeh} and multi-type dynamic epistemic logic
\citep{agt-FrittellaEtAl} provide accounts of information change. In this paper a
recipient's observation map determines which states it can distinguish. Public
restriction changes the space of possible states, and a witnessed transition
supplies the event of a general update. This separation lets us compare the
information an abstract update prescribes with the signal a protocol actually
delivers.

Sheaf-based game semantics investigates the amalgamation of local
strategies \citep{HirschowitzEtAl2008}; interaction sheaves study
coalitional power \citep{AbdouKeiding2009}, and local-to-global decision
models expose obstructions to reconstructing joint choices
\citep{TohmeCaterinaGangle2017,TohmeFioriti2024}.
Sheaf semantics for public announcements and the topological treatment
of distributed epistemic tasks provide related comparisons
\citep{Kishida2013,GoubaultLedentRajsbaum2021,FelberEtAl2025}.
Here causal patches are chosen to detect the dependencies and finite
inconsistencies of secured matching, while owner-scope covers detect
when a policy permitted by each local inspection is nevertheless
prohibited jointly.  These are distinct sites and distinct gluing
questions; neither replaces the original dependent Set doctrine.
The owner-scope site has vanishing higher abelian sheaf cohomology
(\cref{cor:egt-owner-scope-cohomology}). The economic cohomology
constructions therefore use decision incidences and legal-deviation
graphs instead. The former retains actual local responses and admits
an exact affine obstruction, in comparison with the section and
cohomological approaches to contextuality
\citep{AbramskyBrandenburger2011,AbramskyMansfieldBarbosa2012}.
The latter connects graph-flow potential analysis
\citep{CandoganEtAl2011} to coupled legality, execution prices, and
whole-owner delegation. The finite interaction-array argument proves
robust-solvability statements directly on the legal subobject; it does
not infer independent feasibility of coalition and outsider choices
from a product-game presentation.

The Hennessy--Milner separation theorem
\citep{HennessyMilner1980,HennessyMilner1985} provides the modal precedent for
testing behaviour in finitely branching systems. Our tests observe the designated
epistemic, deviation, and witnessed transition relations. On a finite retained
frame, characteristic formulas then distinguish exactly the classes of its
behavioural equivalence.

Three comparisons account for the passage from the categorical ingredients to claims
about agency. The legal lift of \cref{lem:ownerwise-legal-lifting} realizes an
alternative while keeping the reference outsiders fixed. The protocol of
\cref{thm:egt-causal-protocol} realizes a decision with its causal prerequisites.
The back-lifts of \cref{thm:egt-announcement-policy-comparison} recover strategic
and epistemic alternatives from a public message at the given source. The underlying
copower, internal-hom, and Yoneda identities give the representation. These
comparisons establish what an owner can still do or distinguish when that
representation changes.

\noindent\textbf{Use of AI-assisted tools.} Generative AI systems were used during the research and development of this manuscript. Responsibility for the mathematical content, arguments, and conclusions rests with the author.

\part{Concurrent semantics and first-class agents}

\section{True-Concurrent Games and Dependent Linear Semantics}\label{sec:paper-1}

A checker can wait for two decisions without requiring either agent to move first.
To describe such a protocol, we need a model that records a dependency where a
component waits and leaves independent events unordered. Polarized event structures
and the secured composition of \citet{CastellanEtAl2017} provide this model. We
first build finite value and collection protocols to identify the barriers they
impose. We then use restricted Yoneda and Day convolution to introduce the sums,
products, and ordinary parameters needed for dependent agent types. The embedding
recovers every original concurrent arrow, so these additional operations preserve
the causal account of execution.

\subsection{Operational event structures and concurrent interaction}
\label{sec:egt-interaction}

\subsubsection{Concurrent histories}

\begin{definition}[Event structures and configurations]
\label{def:egt-event-structures-and-configurations}
An \textbf{event} is one occurrence of an action or communication, so two
occurrences of the same kind of action remain distinct events.
\textbf{True concurrency} records prerequisites and compatibility directly,
without first choosing a total schedule for independent events. In the
formal data below, a down-closed set contains every prerequisite of each
of its events. An event is \textbf{enabled} after a configuration $x$ when
$e\notin x$ and $x\cup\{e\}$ is again a configuration. Two distinct events are concurrent
when they can occur together and neither causally precedes the other;
incompatible collections are in conflict. The consistency family also
records incompatibilities involving more than two events.

An \textbf{event structure} is a triple $E=(|E|,\leq_E,\operatorname{Con}_E)$.
The relation $\leq_E$ is a partial order with finite principal downsets.
The family $\operatorname{Con}_E$ consists of finite subsets of $|E|$, contains the
empty set and every singleton, is closed under subsets, and satisfies
\[
 X\in\operatorname{Con}_E,\quad e\leq_E e'\in X
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad X\cup\{e\}\in\operatorname{Con}_E.
\]
A finite \textbf{configuration} is a down-closed consistent subset.
Write $\operatorname{Conf}(E)$ for the set of finite configurations.
\end{definition}

The order records prerequisites. Consistency records which finite collections
can occur together. Two events can be consistent without either causing the
other. A configuration therefore records a partially ordered history rather
than an arbitrary linear ordering of its independent events.

\begin{construction}[Enabled-event span]
\label{con:egt-enabled-event-span}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Enabled extensions.} For an event structure $E$ put $W_E=\operatorname{Conf}(E)$ and define
\[
 \mathsf{Step}(E)
 =\{(x,e)\in W_E\times|E|:e\notin x,\ x\cup\{e\}\in W_E\}.
\]
It has projections $p(x,e)=x$ and $\ell(x,e)=e$, and a target
$t(x,e)=x\cup\{e\}$.
  \item \textbf{Source and target.} Thus
\[
 W_E\xleftarrow{p}\mathsf{Step}(E)\xrightarrow{t}W_E
\]
is a relation span: $(p,t)$ is jointly injective, since
$e=t(x,e)\setminus x$ is determined by its two endpoints. The inclusion
$\mathsf{Step}(E)\hookrightarrow W_E\times|E|$ is the comprehension
of the event-enablement predicate.
  \item \textbf{Execution in a configuration.} Every event of a finite configuration
can be executed in some linear extension of that configuration's causal
order, but the span does not choose a linear extension.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

\noindent The incidence inclusion and source projection give the enabled-event diagram.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
\mathsf{Step}(E) \arrow[r,hook,"\iota"] \arrow[dr,"p"']
 & W_E\times |E| \arrow[d,"\pi_1"] \\
 & W_E
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Stealth, every node/.style={font=\small},
  event/.style={draw,rounded corners,inner sep=6pt}]
\node[event] (a) at (0,0) {commit $A$};
\node[event] (b) at (3.6,0) {commit $B$};
\node[event] (c) at (1.8,-1.3) {settle};
\draw[->] (a)--(c); \draw[->] (b)--(c);
\node[align=center,text width=9cm] at (1.8,-2.35)
  {Neither commitment orders the other. Settlement depends on both.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Causal dependence without a scheduler-imposed order.}
\label{fig:egt-concurrency}
\end{figure}

\begin{definition}[Total event-structure map]
\label{def:egt-total-event-structure-map}
For event structures $E,F$, a \textbf{total map of event structures} is a
function $f:|E|\to|F|$ satisfying, for every finite configuration
$x\in\operatorname{Conf}(E)$,
\[
 f[x]\in\operatorname{Conf}(F),\qquad
 f|_x:x\longrightarrow f[x]\text{ is injective}.
\]
It thus preserves configurations and is locally injective. It need not
preserve every source causal order as an order relation between event
labels: a strategy may add dependencies specifying when it responds.
\end{definition}
\begin{definition}[Polarized arenas]
\label{def:egt-polarized-arenas}
The polarity is relative to an interaction boundary: negative events are
moves the surrounding interaction may supply, and positive events are moves
the strategy may make. Reversing an interface reverses these roles. Economic ownership is recorded by the separate owner-indexed policy signature. For example,
several players' chosen messages can all be positive outputs of separate
components, while becoming negative inputs of the component that receives
them.

An \textbf{arena} is an event structure with a polarity
$\operatorname{pol}:|A|\to\{-,+\}$. Its dual $A^\perp$ reverses polarities.
The parallel arena $A\parallel B$ is the disjoint union, with componentwise
causality and consistency. The empty arena is denoted $I$.
\end{definition}

\subsubsection{Strategies and their composition}

An output and an input at a shared interface can synchronize only if their combined
prerequisites admit a causal order. The synchronization pullback records the secured
history for each match. Two matches with identical visible labels may therefore
remain distinct when their histories are incompatible.

We use the secured-bijection pullback of \citet{CastellanEtAl2017}.
Its universal property supplies the synchronization object subsequently
used in interaction and hiding.

\begin{definition}[Secured matching]
\label{def:egt-secured-matching}
Let $f:S\to A$ and $g:T\to A$ be total maps of unpolarized event
structures. A matching is a finite graph $\varphi\subseteq |S|\times|T|$
whose projections are configurations, which is the graph of a bijection
between those configurations, and for which $f(s)=g(t)$ whenever
$(s,t)\in\varphi$. Order its pairs by the transitive closure of
\[
 (s,t)\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}(s',t')
 \quad\text{if}\quad s\leq_S s'\text{ or }t\leq_T t'.
\]
The matching is secured when this closure is antisymmetric. It is prime
when this finite partial order has a greatest pair. Write
$\mathcal M(f,g)$ and $\mathcal M_\bullet(f,g)$ for the secured and
prime secured matchings.
\end{definition}

\begin{construction}[Synchronization object]
\label{con:egt-pullback}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Events and order.} The events of $\mathsf{Sync}(f,g)$ are $\mathcal M_\bullet(f,g)$, ordered by
inclusion.
  \item \textbf{Consistency.} A finite set of primes is consistent precisely when its
union is a secured matching.
  \item \textbf{Projections.} A prime is projected to the coordinates
of its greatest pair, giving maps $p:\mathsf{Sync}(f,g)\to S$ and $q:\mathsf{Sync}(f,g)\to T$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

\noindent The pullback compares the two occurrences proposed for synchronization by
their images at the shared interface.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
& \mathsf{Sync}(f,g) \arrow[dl,"q"']\arrow[dr,"p"] & \\
 T \arrow[dr,"g"'] && S \arrow[dl,"f"] \\
 & A &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{theorem}[Synchronization universal property; recalled]
\label{thm:egt-pullback}
The construction is an event structure, with a bijection
\[
 \operatorname{Conf}(\mathsf{Sync}(f,g))\cong\mathcal M(f,g),
 \qquad X\longmapsto\bigcup X.
\]
The maps $p,q$ exhibit it as the pullback of $f,g$ in the category of
event structures and total maps.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Source and identification]
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Secured operational interaction.} This is the secured-bijection pullback theorem of
\citet{CastellanEtAl2017}. In the notation fixed above, a secured
matching $\varphi$ determines the configuration
\[
 X_\varphi=\{\downarrow_\varphi u:u\in\varphi\}
\]
of prime secured matchings, and a configuration $X$ of primes recovers the
secured matching $\bigcup X$. These operations are inverse.
  \item \textbf{Lifting through the comparison.} The maps $p$
and $q$ take a prime to the coordinates of its greatest pair, and the
cited pullback theorem identifies the unique lift of a cone with the prime
secured histories generated by its configurations. We use that universal
property below; no different synchronization construction is introduced
here.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
V \arrow[dr,dashed,"\ell"] \arrow[drr,bend left=16,"h"]
  \arrow[ddr,bend right=16,"k"'] & & \\
& \mathsf{Sync}(f,g) \arrow[r,"p"] \arrow[d,"q"'] & S \arrow[d,"f"] \\
& T \arrow[r,"g"'] & A
\end{tikzcd}
\caption{Prime secured histories supply the synchronization pullback.}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Locality of secured synchronization.}
A secured interaction has partially visible causal histories even before hiding.
The following site makes those partial histories precise.  In contrast with a
cover by arbitrary event labels, a cover must expose the causal predecessors
and the finite incompatibilities relevant to the synchronization.  The
resulting descent theorem is specific to secured event-structure pullbacks;
it is not a sheafification of the Day completion introduced below.  The
local-strategy viewpoint of \citet{HirschowitzEtAl2008} motivates this
question, while the operational pullback remains the one of
\citet{CastellanEtAl2017}.

\begin{construction}[Causally saturated site of a synchronization]
\label{con:sheaf-causal-site}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Form the causal patches.} Fix total event-structure maps
$f:S\to E$ and $g:T\to E$.  Let $\mathcal O_{f,g}$ be the poset of
subsets $U\subseteq |E|$ satisfying
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 e'\leq_E e\in U&\Longrightarrow e'\in U,\\
 s'\leq_S s,\ f(s)\in U&\Longrightarrow f(s')\in U,\\
 t'\leq_T t,\ g(t)\in U&\Longrightarrow g(t')\in U.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Write $S_U=S|_{f^{-1}U}$, $T_U=T|_{g^{-1}U}$, and $E_U=E|_U$,
with inherited order and consistency.  The restricted maps
$f_U:S_U\to E_U$ and $g_U:T_U\to E_U$ are total event-structure maps.
  \item \textbf{Detect finite incompatibility.} A finite subset
$F\subseteq|S_U|$ is \emph{minimally inconsistent} when
$F\notin\operatorname{Con}_{S_U}$ and every proper subset belongs to
$\operatorname{Con}_{S_U}$.  Use the analogous definition in $T_U$.
  \item \textbf{Specify covers.} A covering family of $U$ is a
\emph{nonempty finite} family $(U_j\subseteq U)_{j\in J}$ of saturated
patches such that $U=\bigcup_jU_j$ and every minimally inconsistent
finite set $F$ in $S_U$, respectively $T_U$, has its whole label set
$f[F]$, respectively $g[F]$, contained in one $U_j$.
At $U=\varnothing$ the identity family is a cover; the empty family
is not declared covering.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

\begin{lemma}[Pretopology and valid restrictions]
\label{lem:sheaf-causal-pretopology}
The covering families of Construction~\ref{con:sheaf-causal-site} form a
Grothendieck pretopology.  Restriction of a secured matching to a saturated
patch is a secured matching, and restrictions compose strictly.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Restriction of maps and configurations.} The inverse
images of $U$ in $S,T$ are downward closed by saturation.  Therefore
every configuration of $S_U$ or $T_U$ is a configuration of the original
structure.  Configuration preservation and local injectivity of $f_U,g_U$
follow from those of $f,g$.  Intersecting a matching graph with pairs
whose common label lies in $U$ keeps downward-closed configurations;
the induced secured order is a restriction of the original acyclic order.
  \item \textbf{Identity and base change.} The identity cover detects every
minimal inconsistency.  If $V\subseteq U$ is saturated and $(U_j)$
covers $U$, then $(V\cap U_j)$ covers $V$: a minimally inconsistent
set in $S_V$ or $T_V$ is also minimally inconsistent in $S_U$ or $T_U$,
so the covering member that contains its labels continues to do so
upon intersection with $V$.
  \item \textbf{Transitivity.} If each $U_j$ is covered by $(U_{jk})$,
a minimal inconsistent set over $U$ first has all its labels in some
$U_j$, where it remains minimally inconsistent; it then has all its
labels in some $U_{jk}$.  The composite finite family covers the
underlying events.  All families remain nonempty, including at the
empty patch.  Intersection of restrictions is strict.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{construction}[The secured-matching sheaf]
\label{con:sheaf-matching}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Assign local matchings.} Define
\[
 \mathscr M_{f,g}(U)=\mathcal M(f_U,g_U).
\]
For $V\subseteq U$ saturated, restrict a matching $\varphi$ to
$\varphi|_V=\{(s,t)\in\varphi:f(s)=g(t)\in V\}$.
  \item \textbf{Retain the empty history.} There is a unique matching
on the empty patch, and its restriction is the empty graph.  This
records the absence of matched events, not an arbitrary choice of a
linear schedule.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

\begin{theorem}[Sheaf descent for secured matchings]
\label{thm:sheaf-secured-gluing}
For every covering family $(U_j)_{j\in J}$ of $U$, restriction gives a
natural bijection
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sheaf-secured-equalizer}
 \mathscr M_{f,g}(U)\;\cong\;
 \operatorname{Eq}\left(
 \prod_j\mathscr M_{f,g}(U_j)
 \rightrightarrows
 \prod_{j,k}\mathscr M_{f,g}(U_j\cap U_k)\right).
\end{equation}
In particular $\mathscr M_{f,g}$ is a sheaf for the displayed
Grothendieck pretopology.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Amalgamate a matching family.} For compatible secured
matchings $(\varphi_j)$ set $\varphi=\bigcup_j\varphi_j$.
This graph is finite.  If the same $s$ were paired with different
$t,t'$, the common label $f(s)=g(t)=g(t')$ belongs to the intersection
of their patches, and compatibility there forces $t=t'$.  The
analogous argument proves injectivity of the other projection.  Thus
$\varphi$ is the graph of a bijection and $\varphi|_{U_j}=\varphi_j$.
  \item \textbf{Recover causal closure.} A predecessor $s'\leq_Ss$
of any $s$ appearing in $\varphi_j$ has its label in $U_j$ by
saturation, and belongs to the configuration projected from
$\varphi_j$.  The union's source projection is therefore downward
closed.  Likewise for the target projection.
  \item \textbf{Recover finite consistency.} If the finite source
projection were inconsistent, it would contain a minimally inconsistent
finite subset $F$.  Some patch $U_j$ contains all of $f[F]$, so
$F\subseteq\operatorname{pr}_S(\varphi_j)$, contradicting consistency.
The argument for the target projection is identical.  Both projections
are thus configurations.
  \item \textbf{Recover securedness.} A cycle in the transitive closure
of the combined source and target causal orders on $\varphi$ has a finite
cycle of matched pairs.  Choose a patch containing one pair.  Along
each causal edge, saturation forces the preceding pair into any patch
containing the succeeding pair.  Traversing the cycle backwards puts
all its pairs in the chosen patch.  This contradicts the securedness
of $\varphi_j$.  Hence the global matching is secured.
  \item \textbf{Prove uniqueness and naturality.} Every pair in any
global amalgamation is supported in a covering patch, where its value
is prescribed.  Its graph must be $\bigcup_j\varphi_j$.  Union and
restriction are inverse.  Passing to a smaller saturated patch commutes
with both constructions, proving naturality.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\noindent The sheaf equalizer records agreement on all pairwise causal overlaps.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
\mathscr M_{f,g}(U)\arrow[r,hook,"\mathrm{res}"]&
 \displaystyle\prod_j\mathscr M_{f,g}(U_j)
 \arrow[r,shift left=.7ex,"r_1"]
 \arrow[r,shift right=.7ex,"r_2"']&
 \displaystyle\prod_{j,k}\mathscr M_{f,g}(U_j\cap U_k)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{theorem}[Reconstruction of secured interaction]
\label{thm:sheaf-sync-reconstruction}
For the synchronization pullback $P=\mathsf{Sync}(f,g)$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:egt-pullback},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sheaf-sync-sections}
 \Gamma(\mathscr M_{f,g})\cong\mathcal M(f,g)
 \cong\operatorname{Conf}(P).
\end{equation}
The same sections recover the prime events, order, and consistency:
\[
 |P|=\mathcal M_\bullet(f,g),\qquad
 p\leq_Pq\iff p\subseteq q,\qquad
 \{p_1,\ldots,p_n\}\in\operatorname{Con}_P
 \iff\bigcup_jp_j\in\mathcal M(f,g).
\]
For parallel pairs of matching maps, restriction to componentwise
patches satisfies the natural product comparison
\[
 \mathscr M_{f\parallel f',\,g\parallel g'}(U\sqcup U')
 \cong\mathscr M_{f,g}(U)\times\mathscr M_{f',g'}(U').
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Recover global sections.} The full carrier $|E|$
is terminal in the site.  A natural section is determined by its
value there and its restrictions, giving the first bijection.
The second is the secured-pullback correspondence in
Theorem~\ref{thm:egt-pullback}.  Prime secured matchings are the
principal histories generated by greatest pairs, with the displayed
order and finite-consistency test.  Thus reconstruction retains the
actual event structure, not just a set of linear extensions.
  \item \textbf{Prove the product comparison.} No matched pair in a
disjoint-union interface can cross between its two summands.  A
matching splits uniquely into one matching in each summand; source and
target configurations and the absence of causal cycles are componentwise.
Disjoint union is the inverse.  Intersections and restrictions of
componentwise patches commute with this bijection.
  \item \textbf{Recover composition.} In the manuscript's sequential
interaction, apply the theorem to the augmented maps into
$A^\perp\parallel B\parallel C$, then apply the existing hiding
operation to the reconstructed secured pullback.  The result is the
original composite, so the already proved associativity, copycat and
interchange equations apply unchanged.  This claim is about
reconstruction of interaction, not a new monoidal closed structure on
the sheaf category.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[A concurrent gluing and two failed covers]
\label{ex:sheaf-causal-covers}
For the identity maps on the event structure $c<a$, $c<b$ with $a,b$
independent, the patches $\{c,a\}$ and $\{c,b\}$ cover.  Their
compatible identity matchings glue to the five configurations
$\varnothing$, $\{c\}$, $\{c,a\}$, $\{c,b\}$, $\{c,a,b\}$; neither
schedule $c,a,b$ nor $c,b,a$ is chosen.

The causal and consistency conditions on covers are essential.
If the arena has two independent labels $a,b$, while one source orders
$a<b$ and the other orders $b<a$, the two singleton identity-labelled
matchings would glue along an arbitrary label cover to a causal cycle.
Those singleton patches are not saturated.  If instead $a,b$ are
conflicting in both sources with no order, the singleton patches are
saturated but their local matchings have an inconsistent union; they
fail the minimal-inconsistency covering test.  These are counterexamples
to the naive label-cover sheaf condition.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[Prime events are recovered after gluing]
A prime matching need not restrict to a prime matching.  For instance,
if independent $a,b$ both precede $c$, the prime history with greatest
pair labelled $c$ restricts to the nonprime history $\{a,b\}$ on the
saturated patch $\{a,b\}$.  Thus the sheaf stores secured matching
configurations; its prime events are reconstructed by
Theorem~\ref{thm:sheaf-sync-reconstruction}.  General presheaves in
$\widehat{\mathcal C}$ and sheaves on $\mathcal O_{f,g}$ serve distinct
purposes.
\end{remark}


\begin{definition}[Concurrent strategy]
\label{def:egt-concurrent-strategy}
Receptivity requires a unique extension in the strategy for the arrival of
each enabled negative event. Courtesy permits the strategy to wait for an
input before producing an output, but prevents it from inserting arbitrary
new dependencies between moves whose ordering is already controlled by the
arena. Here $e\lessdot e'$ means an immediate causal dependency, with no
event strictly between them. Thus a protocol may wait for both submitted
messages before announcing their joint outcome without imposing an order
between the two submissions.

A concurrent strategy from $A$ to $B$ is a polarity-preserving total map
\[
 s:S\longrightarrow A^\perp\parallel B
\]
with two conditions. \textbf{Receptivity} says that every enabled negative move
has a unique extension in the strategy. More explicitly, if $x$ is a
configuration of $S$ and $s(x)\cup\{a\}$ is a configuration extending $s(x)$ by
a negative event, there is a unique $e$ with $s(e)=a$ and
$x\cup\{e\}\in\operatorname{Conf}(S)$. \textbf{Courtesy} says that a new immediate
dependency may only run from a negative event to a positive event. Thus, if
$e\mathrel{\lessdot}_S e'$ and either $\operatorname{pol}(e)=+$ or
$\operatorname{pol}(e')=-$, then $s(e)\mathrel{\lessdot}s(e')$ in the arena.
\end{definition}

\begin{construction}[Secured interaction and hiding]
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Synchronize the shared interface.} For strategies $S\to A^\perp\parallel B$ and
$T\to B^\perp\parallel C$, interaction synchronizes the occurrences on $B$.
Only \textbf{secured} synchronizations are admitted: the combined causal orders
of the matched histories must be acyclic.
  \item \textbf{Hide the internal events.} Composition then hides the matched
$B$-events while retaining the induced order on visible events. The
acyclicity condition prevents a circular collection of unfulfilled
prerequisites from being mistaken for a possible interaction.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
& S\mathbin{\circledast_B}T \arrow[dl,dashed] \arrow[dr,dashed]
  \arrow[d,dashed,"\text{hide }B"] & \\
S \arrow[d] & T\odot S \arrow[d] & T \arrow[d] \\
A^\perp\parallel B & A^\perp\parallel C & B^\perp\parallel C
\end{tikzcd}
\caption{Interaction precedes hiding. Dashed arrows are partial maps of
event structures: projection forgets events private to the other component,
and hiding forgets internal events. Solid arrows are total strategy maps.}
\end{figure}

\begin{theorem}[Concurrent composition; imported]
\label{thm:egt-base}
Polarized event structures and receptive courteous strategies, taken up to
isomorphism over their arenas, form a compact closed category $\mathcal C$.
Composition is secured interaction followed by hiding, identity is copycat,
tensor is parallel composition, and duality reverses polarity.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Reference and size verification]
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Composition.} For composition and compact closure, see
\citet{CastellanEtAl2017}. Parallel composition, finite secured histories,
and hiding preserve countability. On a fixed countable carrier, orders,
consistency families, polarities, and labellings range over sets.
  \item \textbf{Causal execution.} Taking a
set of countable carriers and quotienting strategy presentations by
isomorphism therefore gives a set $\mathcal C(A,B)$ for every $A,B$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{notation}[Compact structure]
We write $\otimes$ for parallel composition in $\mathcal C$ and $I$ for the
empty arena. Arena-preserving strategy isomorphisms represent equality of
arrows. Put
\[
 \widetilde\eta_A=
 I\xrightarrow{\eta_A}A^\perp\otimes A
 \xrightarrow{\gamma}A\otimes A^\perp.
\]
Interaction polarities are independent of economic ownership.
\end{notation}

\subsubsection{The linear account of interaction}

\begin{construction}[Composition and copycat in the chosen convention]
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Form the interaction.} The preceding pullback describes the interaction used by
Theorem~\ref{thm:egt-base}. Forget the polarities on the shared interface
while forming the pullback of
\[
 S\parallel C\xrightarrow{s\parallel\operatorname{id}}
 A^\perp\parallel B\parallel C
 \xleftarrow{\operatorname{id}\parallel t} A^\perp\parallel T.
\]
The additional factors carry the events private to the other component.
  \item \textbf{Restrict to the exterior arena.} The pullback has a map to the three-interface arena. Keep just its events
labelled in $A^\perp\parallel C$, restrict order and consistency, and
restrict the labelling map. This gives the composite. Restricting the
transitive order retains the visible consequence of an internal causal
chain; it does not simply erase the chain's dependencies.
  \item \textbf{Construct copycat.} The copycat strategy of \citet{CastellanEtAl2017} is constructed as follows: start with the two interface copies of $A$, add
the forwarding edge from the negative occurrence of each arena event to its
positive occurrence, take transitive closure, and define consistency through
the causal closure in the arena. We use the cited verification that this gives
a receptive courteous strategy and that it is the identity for secured
interaction followed by hiding. Thus no separate copycat correctness claim is
being introduced here; the concrete description only fixes the convention
used by the imported compact-closed structure.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

\begin{construction}[The closed structure of concurrent interaction]
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Tensor and internal hom.} The tensor is $A\otimes B=A\parallel B$, with unit the empty arena.
Compact closure constructs the internal hom
$A\multimap B=A^\perp\parallel B$ and the natural bijection
\[
 \mathcal C(X\otimes A,B)\cong\mathcal C(X,A\multimap B).
\]
  \item \textbf{Evaluation and transposition.} Evaluation and transposition are obtained from the displayed cups, caps,
and symmetry. The snake equations prove the inverse laws for this
bijection. Identity is copycat, composition is interaction and hiding,
and tensor places interactions in parallel.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

Compact closure provides a tensor for combining linear interfaces and an internal
hom for linear interaction, as in \citet{Girard1987}. An agent type also needs an
ordinary parameter that can index several uses of a policy description.
Section~\ref{sec:egt-dependent-semantics} constructs such parameters and the linear
interfaces that depend on them.

\begin{remark}[Related concurrent semantics]
The extension by symmetry and the construction of concurrent Hyland--Ong
games are developed in \citet{CastellanClairambaultWinskel2019}.
\citet{Winskel2023} relates concurrent strategies to functional models,
including lenses and optics. These works situate the chosen operational
category and its functional fragments; the constructions used here are the
ones explicitly specified above and below.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{Ordinary functions as response protocols}

\begin{construction}[Finite value arenas and response strategies]
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Form the value arena.} For a finite set $X$, let $D(X)$ be the positive arena with one event for each
$x\in X$, no nontrivial causal order, and configurations $\varnothing$ and
the singletons. Distinct values conflict.
  \item \textbf{Realize a response.} A function $f:X\to Y$ determines
a strategy $\widehat f:D(X)\to D(Y)$. For each $x$, its corresponding branch
contains a negative input event $x$ and a positive output event labelled
$f(x)$, with the input preceding the output; different input branches
conflict.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

\begin{proposition}
\label{prop:egt-functions}
The assignments $X\mapsto D(X)$ and $f\mapsto\widehat f$ form a faithful
functor from finite sets and functions to $\mathcal C$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Secured operational interaction.} The only added dependency is negative-to-positive, so courtesy holds. At the empty configuration every input is accepted once; after an input,
all other inputs conflict with it in the arena.
  \item \textbf{Receptivity and functional composition.} This proves receptivity. Synchronizing $\widehat f$ and $\widehat g$ produces, on the branch indexed
by $x$, the chain $x\to f(x)\to g(f(x))$. Hiding the middle event gives
$\widehat{g\circ f}$.
  \item \textbf{Secured operational interaction.} For the identity function the construction is copycat
on $D(X)$. Distinct functions differ on an input and therefore on an output
label of the corresponding strategy; they cannot be isomorphic over the
arena.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\noindent The point strategies form a natural family with respect to finite response maps.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
I \arrow[r,"\mathsf{pt}_X(x)"] \arrow[d,equal]
 & D(X)\arrow[d,"\widehat f"] \\
 I\arrow[r,"\mathsf{pt}_Y(f(x))"'] & D(Y)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{notation}[Value states]
For $x\in X$, write
\[
 \mathsf{pt}_X(x):I\longrightarrow D(X)
\]
for the one-event positive strategy selecting $x$. Equivalently, if
$\bar x:1\to X$ is the corresponding function and
$\upsilon:I\to D(1)$ is the unique one-event state, then
\[
 \mathsf{pt}_X(x)=\widehat{\bar x}\circ\upsilon.
\]
Functoriality gives the naturality equation
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:egt-value-state-naturality}
 \widehat f\circ\mathsf{pt}_X(x)
 =\mathsf{pt}_Y(f(x)).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, under $X\cong\mathbf{FinSet}(1,X)$, the functions
$\mathsf{pt}_X:X\to\mathcal C(I,D(X))$ are the components of the
natural transformation
\[
 \mathsf{pt}:\mathbf{FinSet}(1,-)
 \Longrightarrow \mathcal C(I,D(-)),
\]
between functors $\mathbf{FinSet}\to\mathbf{Set}$.
Its construction is the hom-functor action of $D$ on
$X\cong\mathbf{FinSet}(1,X)$, followed by precomposition with
$\upsilon$. The symbol denotes a selected point of a data arena and is
separate from both compact coevaluation $\eta_A$ and later quotation.
\end{notation}

A recipient of $D(X\times Y)$ receives one report containing both values. A recipient of
$D(X)\otimes D(Y)$ can receive either output first. Faithfulness records the distinctions
between the original response maps. Collecting independent outputs into a joint
report imposes a further requirement. The collector must wait for both, which
determines when a later policy may first use both values.

\subsubsection{Communication of data and synchronization barriers}

\begin{construction}[Copying and disposal of data]
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Specify the data maps.} For data that may be reported to several recipients there are explicit
copying and disposal strategies
\[
 \Delta_X:D(X)\to D(X)\otimes D(X),\qquad
 \epsilon_X:D(X)\to I.
\]
  \item \textbf{Copy an input.} The source of $\Delta_X$ has, for each value $x$, one negative input
and two independent positive outputs, each labelled $x$ and each
dependent on the input. Different input branches conflict.
  \item \textbf{Dispose of an input.} The source
of $\epsilon_X$ is just the negative input arena. These are receptive
and courteous by direct inspection: every input is accepted uniquely,
and the only new dependencies are negative-to-positive.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

\begin{proposition}[Duplicable data]
\label{prop:egt-data-comonoid}
The triple $(D(X),\Delta_X,\epsilon_X)$ is a commutative comonoid
in $\mathcal C$. For every finite function $f:X\to Y$,
\[
 (\widehat f\otimes\widehat f)\Delta_X
   =\Delta_Y\widehat f,\qquad
 \epsilon_Y\widehat f=\epsilon_X.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Associativity.} Both bracketings of the iterated copy strategy have, after interaction
and hiding, one negative input event labelled $x$ and three independent
positive output events labelled $x$, each with that input as its
prerequisite. Matching corresponding events gives an isomorphism over
the arena.
  \item \textbf{Copying comonoid laws.} This proves coassociativity, including its prescribed
associators. Swapping the two outputs is a branchwise isomorphism,
proving cocommutativity. Composing either output with disposal leaves
one input and its single copied output, exactly copycat. This proves
the two counit equations.
  \item \textbf{Causal execution.} For the naturality equation, each side has an input branch for $x$
and two independent outputs labelled $f(x)$. Their only visible causal
prerequisite is the input. The branchwise identification is again an
isomorphism.
  \item \textbf{Secured operational interaction.} Discarding the output of $\widehat f$ leaves just its
receptive input behavior, which is $\epsilon_X$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\noindent Naturality of copying is expressed by the following commuting square.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
D(X)\arrow[r,"\Delta_X"]\arrow[d,"\widehat f"']
 & D(X)\otimes D(X)\arrow[d,"\widehat f\otimes\widehat f"] \\
 D(Y)\arrow[r,"\Delta_Y"'] & D(Y)\otimes D(Y)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Copying and disposal are designated operations on these finite data
interfaces, not structural rules of the linear syntax. An isomorphism in
the ambient concurrent category can transport a comonoid structure, so
material nonduplicability cannot be inferred from an object's isomorphism
class alone. Material feasibility and authorization are instead tracked by
exhibited certificates and witnessed institutional executions, as constructed
in Section~\ref{sec:egt-witnesses}; an ambient morphism alone does not
establish either property. Thus communication may copy a signal without
thereby certifying another authorization or resource occurrence.

\begin{construction}[Distribution of a paired value]
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Distribute a paired input.} There is also a distributor
$d_{X,Y}:D(X\times Y)\to D(X)\otimes D(Y)$. For each pair $(x,y)$ its
source has one negative input labelled $(x,y)$ and two independent positive
outputs labelled $x$ and $y$, both following that input. Different paired
inputs conflict.
  \item \textbf{Verify the strategy conditions.} It is receptive and courteous by the same direct check as the
response protocols above.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

A collector must accommodate partially received tuples. Completed
tuples sharing a channel value therefore share the corresponding negative
input event, rather than generating incompatible copies of that input.
The canonical collector below makes this sharing explicit.

\begin{construction}[Canonical finite collector]
\label{con:egt-finite-collector}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Form the input and output events.} Let $J$ be a finite index set and let $(X_j)_{j\in J}$ be finite sets. Put
$X_J=\prod_{j\in J}X_j$. Define an event structure $C_{\mathbf X}$ with
negative events
\[
 e_{j,x}\qquad(j\in J,\ x\in X_j)
\]
and positive events
\[
 o_{\mathbf x}\qquad(\mathbf x=(x_j)_{j\in J}\in X_J).
\]
  \item \textbf{Generate order and consistency.} Generate its causal order by
\[
 e_{j,x_j}<o_{\mathbf x}\qquad(j\in J).
\]
A finite set of events is consistent precisely when it contains at most one
input value on each component, at most one tuple output, and every input that
occurs together with $o_{\mathbf x}$ has the value prescribed by
$\mathbf x$.
  \item \textbf{Label the collector.} Label $e_{j,x}$ by the input occurrence $x$ on component $j$
and label $o_{\mathbf x}$ by the tuple $\mathbf x$. Denote the resulting map
by
\[
 c_{\mathbf X}:C_{\mathbf X}\longrightarrow
 \left(\bigotimes_{j\in J}D(X_j)\right)^\perp
 \parallel D(X_J).
\]
For $J=\{1,2\}$ write $c_{X,Y}$, and for $J=\varnothing$ write
$c_0:I\to D(1)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

\begin{proposition}[Finite collectors]
\label{prop:egt-finite-collectors}
The map $c_{\mathbf X}$ is a receptive courteous strategy
\[
 c_{X_j\,|\,j\in J}:
 \bigotimes_{j\in J}D(X_j)
 \longrightarrow
 D\!\left(\prod_{j\in J}X_j\right).
\]
A configuration containing the tuple output $o_{\mathbf x}$ contains exactly
its required input events $e_{j,x_j}$ in their causal past. Every iterated
binary collector, followed by the canonical reassociation of the Cartesian
product, is isomorphic to this strategy over its arena. The nullary collector
$c_0$ is the one-event positive state selecting the empty tuple.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Causal execution.} A principal downset of an input event is a singleton, while
\[
 \downarrow o_{\mathbf x}
 =\{o_{\mathbf x}\}\cup\{e_{j,x_j}:j\in J\},
\]
so principal downsets are finite. Consistency is downward closed. For the
cause-extension axiom, the only nontrivial case is
$e_{j,x_j}\leq o_{\mathbf x}$ with $o_{\mathbf x}$ already in a consistent
set.
  \item \textbf{Causal execution: second comparison.} Such a set cannot contain a different input value on component $j$;
therefore adjoining $e_{j,x_j}$ preserves consistency. Thus
$C_{\mathbf X}$ is an event structure.
  \item \textbf{Causal execution.} A configuration containing $o_{\mathbf x}$ is down-closed, hence contains all
$e_{j,x_j}$, and its image is a configuration of the arrow arena. A
configuration without an output contains at most one value on each input
component. The labelling is injective on either kind of configuration, so it
is a total map of event structures.
  \item \textbf{Secured operational interaction.} For receptivity, let $z$ be a source configuration and suppose that the arrow
arena enables a negative input $x\in X_j$. Then $z$ contains no input on
component $j$. It cannot contain a tuple output either, because down-closure of
such an output would already contain an input on component $j$.
  \item \textbf{Collector receptivity and courtesy.} Hence
$z\cup\{e_{j,x}\}$ is a configuration. The source has exactly one event with
that arena label, so the lift is unique. Every added causal edge is of the form
$e_{j,x_j}<o_{\mathbf x}$, hence is negative-to-positive; courtesy follows.
  \item \textbf{Secured operational interaction.} Now expand any iterated binary collector before hiding its intermediate tuple
events. On a completed tuple $\mathbf x$, the visible source events are the
original inputs $e_{j,x_j}$ and the final tuple output. The internal tuple
events form a directed tree from those inputs to the final output, so secured
interaction is acyclic.
  \item \textbf{Secured operational interaction: second comparison.} Hiding the internal tuple events leaves
$e_{j,x_j}<o_{\mathbf x}$ for every $j$ and adds no order between distinct
inputs. Its visible consistency condition is exactly the one in
Construction~\ref{con:egt-finite-collector}. Matching equally labelled
visible events therefore gives an isomorphism over the arena.
  \item \textbf{Causal execution.} Cartesian
coherence identifies every parenthesization with the same product tuple. The
nullary case has no negative events and one positive event labelled by the
unique element of $1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[Lax symmetric-monoidal data interface]
\label{prop:egt-data-lax-monoidal}
The faithful functor $D:\mathbf{FinSet}\to\mathcal C$ of
Proposition~\ref{prop:egt-functions}, together with
\[
 c_{X,Y}:D(X)\otimes D(Y)\to D(X\times Y),
 \qquad c_0:I\to D(1),
\]
is lax symmetric monoidal. Its canonical $J$-ary comparison maps are the
finite collectors of Proposition~\ref{prop:egt-finite-collectors}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Coherence of finite collectors.} The associativity and unit diagrams compare two iterated collectors with the
same finite collector; Proposition~\ref{prop:egt-finite-collectors} supplies
the required isomorphisms, and their coherence is the coherence of Cartesian
reassociation together with symmetric-monoidal coherence in $\mathcal C$. Symmetry exchanges the input components and sends a tuple to its permuted
tuple, giving the symmetry diagram branchwise.
  \item \textbf{Causal execution.} For functions
$f_j:X_j\to Y_j$, both composites
\[
 \widehat{\prod_jf_j}\circ c_{X_j\,|\,j\in J}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 c_{Y_j\,|\,j\in J}\circ\bigotimes_j\widehat f_j
\]
have one input event $e_{j,x}$ for each supplied coordinate and one final
output labelled $(f_j(x_j))_j$, depending on all of those inputs. After
hiding the intermediate response events they are isomorphic over the arena. This proves naturality and the lax symmetric-monoidal laws.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\noindent The lax monoidal structure records the naturality of finite collection.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
D(X)\otimes D(Y)\arrow[r,"c_{X,Y}"]\arrow[d,"\widehat f\otimes\widehat g"']
 & D(X\times Y)\arrow[d,"\widehat{f\times g}"] \\
 D(X')\otimes D(Y')\arrow[r,"c_{X',Y'}"'] & D(X'\times Y')
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{proposition}[The synchronization barrier]
\label{prop:egt-barrier}
One has
\[
 c_{X,Y}\circ d_{X,Y}=\operatorname{id}_{D(X\times Y)}.
\]
For nonempty $X,Y$, the reverse composite is not the identity on
$D(X)\otimes D(Y)$: each of its outputs depends on both inputs.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Secured operational interaction.} In the first composite there is one negative input pair and, after hiding its
two distributed occurrences, one positive output carrying the same pair. Its
source is copycat on $D(X\times Y)$.
  \item \textbf{Reverse implication.} In the reverse composite the collector's
tuple output requires both independent input events. Each distributed output
therefore inherits both prerequisites after hiding. In identity copycat on
$D(X)\otimes D(Y)$, the first positive output can occur after its own negative
input alone, before the second input.
  \item \textbf{Secured operational interaction.} Choosing any values in the two nonempty
sets exhibits a configuration present in copycat and absent from
$d_{X,Y}\circ c_{X,Y}$, so the two strategies are not isomorphic over their
arena.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\noindent Collection and distribution determine a retraction onto paired data.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
D(X\times Y) \arrow[r,"d_{X,Y}"]\arrow[dr,"\id"']
 & D(X)\otimes D(Y)\arrow[d,"c_{X,Y}"] \\
 & D(X\times Y)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The retraction identifies one paired report with the completed
collection of two channels. Its reverse retains the synchronization
barrier: neither output can be forwarded before both inputs have arrived.
This causal difference persists in protocols that make decisions between
individual submissions and completion of a joint report.

\subsection{Dependent completion of concurrent interfaces}
\label{sec:egt-dependent-semantics}

An owned interaction starts from the policy sets $\Sigma_i$ and a
realization $g:\prod_i\Sigma_i\to\mathcal C(A,B)$ in the concurrent
category $\mathcal C$. These form its policy family and concurrent
realization, but these alone do not interpret a policy-dependent boundary
or quantified alternatives. The completion below adds those interfaces
without changing what an arrow between original arenas means. We first
index the operational category by ordinary parameters and then embed it
fully faithfully into a presheaf category with Day tensor. The resulting
indexed linear--nonlinear model will supply agent abstraction and the
logical operations used later.

\subsubsection{Indexed families of true-concurrent interactions}

\begin{construction}[Indexed operational category]
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Index the operational arrows.} The ordinary parameters of an economic model are kept separate from its
linear interfaces. For a set $\Gamma$, let $\mathcal C_\Gamma$ have the same
objects as $\mathcal C$ and hom-sets
\[
 \mathcal C_\Gamma(A,B)
   =\mathbf{Set}\bigl(\Gamma,\mathcal C(A,B)\bigr).
\]
  \item \textbf{Lift composition and tensor.} Composition, tensor, identity, symmetry, cups, and caps are defined
pointwise.
  \item \textbf{Reindex the parameters.} A function $f:\Delta\to\Gamma$ induces reindexing
\[
 f^*:\mathcal C_\Gamma\longrightarrow\mathcal C_\Delta,
 \qquad (f^*t)_\delta=t_{f(\delta)}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

\begin{proposition}[Indexed operational semantics]
\label{prop:egt-indexed-operational}
The assignment $\Gamma\mapsto\mathcal C_\Gamma$ and
$f\mapsto f^*$ is contravariantly functorial. Every fiber
$\mathcal C_\Gamma$ is compact closed with the pointwise structure inherited
from $\mathcal C$, and every reindexing functor preserves that structure.
Thus ordinary parameter substitution and linear interaction form an indexed
compact-closed semantics over $\mathbf{Set}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Monoidal comparison.} Identity and successive reindexing are the identity and associativity laws
for function composition. Every categorical operation is evaluated at one
parameter value at a time, so reindexing commutes with composition and tensor
and sends the constant identity, symmetry, cup, and cap families to the same
constant families. The compact-closed equations therefore hold pointwise in
every fiber because they hold in $\mathcal C$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\noindent Successive parameter substitutions commute with indexed realization.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
\mathcal C_\Gamma \arrow[r,"f^*"]\arrow[dr,"(fg)^*"']
 &\mathcal C_\Delta\arrow[d,"g^*"]\\
 & \mathcal C_\Theta
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{definition}[Owner-indexed parameter category]
\label{def:egt-owner-indexed-parameter-category}
Fix a finite set $N$ of economic agents and put
\[
 \mathbf{Par}_N=\mathbf{Set}^N,
 \qquad
 \Pi_N(\vec\Sigma)=\prod_{i\in N}\Sigma_i.
\]
The product functor $\Pi_N:\mathbf{Par}_N\to\mathbf{Set}$ forgets which
factor is controlled by which owner while retaining the total profile space.
Pulling the indexed operational semantics back along $\Pi_N$ leaves the
true-concurrent operational category unchanged and records exactly the
factorization of ordinary alternatives that will determine deviations.
\end{definition}

\subsubsection{The canonical completion of concurrent interfaces}

Economically, the completion supplies spaces in which policy families,
their dependent alternatives, and predicates can coexist with the original
operational interfaces. Its new objects organize those families; they do
not add new economic decisions to a given arena. Full faithfulness of Yoneda
will ensure that an arrow between original interfaces still denotes exactly
one original concurrent strategy.

\begin{lemma}[Scalars and the obstruction to empty linear limits]
\label{lem:egt-native-empty-obstruction}
The scalar set $\mathcal C(I,I)$ is a singleton. Every arena $A$ has a
state $I\to A$, but $\mathcal C$ has neither an initial nor a terminal
object.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Causal execution.} A total event-structure map to the empty arena has empty source, proving
the scalar assertion. In $A$ take the induced substructure
\[
 A_- = \{e\in A: d\leq_A e\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{pol}(d)=-\}.
\]
It is downward closed. Its inclusion into $A$ is a total event-structure
map and is courteous: an immediate dependency in this downward-closed
substructure is immediate in $A$.
  \item \textbf{Lifting through the comparison.} If a negative event is enabled after
an image configuration, all its strict predecessors belong to that
configuration, so it belongs to $A_-$ and has a unique lift. The inclusion
is therefore a receptive courteous strategy $I\to A$.
  \item \textbf{Causal execution.} If $O$ were initial, its state $s:I\to O$ and the unique $r:O\to I$
would satisfy $rs=1_I$ by scalar uniqueness and $sr=1_O$ by initiality. Then $I$ would be initial. The one-positive-event arena, however, has
distinct empty-source and one-event-source strategies from $I$.
  \item \textbf{Secured operational interaction.} Neither
violates receptivity, and their sources are not isomorphic. This is a
contradiction. Compact duality exchanges initial and terminal objects,
so a terminal object is impossible as well.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}


\begin{convention}[Base, size, and finite ownership]
\label{conv:egt-base}
$\mathbf{Set}$ denotes the ordinary set-theoretic parameter category.
The ambient logic is classical. Predicate calculations use its subobject
doctrine, written with Heyting operations; arguments that use classical order
or finite maximization are identified as such. Set-indexed meets, joins, and
power objects are taken in this base.  The operational category $\mathcal C$ has arbitrary countable
arena carriers. For each fixed pair of arenas, its arrows form the set of
countable strategy presentations whose source carriers are subsets of
$\mathbb N$, modulo arena-preserving isomorphism. Every countable source
admits such a presentation, so this convention retains every operational
arrow. Let $\mathcal C_0$ be the full subcategory on arenas whose event
carriers are subsets of $\mathbb N$, and write
$J:\mathcal C_0\hookrightarrow\mathcal C$ for the inclusion.
The category $\mathcal C_0$ is small. Fixed bijections for finite tagged
carriers equip it with a tensor $\otimes_0$ and coherent comparisons
making $J$ strong symmetric monoidal. The empty arena is its unit $I$.
Every countable arena is isomorphic to some $Jc$ by transport of its
structure along an injection into $\mathbb N$. This is an objectwise
existence statement; no simultaneous choice of representatives is made.
The owner set is a fixed finite list $N$. A coalition $C\subseteq N$
inherits its order from this list, and $-C$ denotes the complementary list.
Thus $\Sigma_C=\prod_{i\in C}\Sigma_i$ retains exactly its members'
controlled coordinates. Empty products are singletons and empty conjunctions
are true; the empty coalition changes no coordinate. Collective improvement
predicates below explicitly quantify over nonempty coalitions.
\end{convention}

An empty dependent linear sum or product requires limits and colimits
not present in the original arena category. We use the small monoidal
category $\mathcal C_0$ and the fully faithful, essentially surjective
inclusion $J:\mathcal C_0\hookrightarrow\mathcal C$ from
Convention~\ref{conv:egt-base}. Presentations with carriers in
$\mathbb N$ retain finite data arenas $D(X)$ and residual arenas
as objects of $\mathcal C$. For each original arena, restricted
Yoneda recovers its concurrent arrows. The new colimits and limits permit
dependent interfaces that the operational arena category itself lacks.
Thus the completion enlarges the language of interfaces, not the possible
executions of any already specified original strategy.

\begin{construction}[Presheaves and Day convolution]
\label{con:egt-day-completion}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=4pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Form the presheaves and their tensor.} Put $\widehat{\mathcal C}=[\mathcal C_0^{\mathrm{op}},\mathbf{Set}]$ and
write $yA=\mathcal C(J(-),A)$ for restricted Yoneda. For presheaves
$P,Q$ and $c\in\mathcal C_0$ define
\[
 (P\otimes_D Q)(c)=
 \int^{a,b\in\mathcal C_0}\mathcal C_0(c,a\otimes_0 b)\times P(a)\times Q(b),
 \qquad \widehat I=yI,
\]
\[
 [P,Q]_D(c)=\operatorname{Nat}\bigl(P,Q(c\otimes_0-)\bigr).
\]
  \item \textbf{Identify coend representatives.} The coend is the quotient of the disjoint union over pairs $(a,b)$ by
the relations induced by arrows in either variable. For example, for
$u:a'\to a$, it identifies $(k,P(u)x,z)$ with
$((u\otimes_0 1)k,x,z)$; the other variable is treated identically.
  \item \textbf{Reindex and take limits.} Reindexing in $c$ is precomposition. Limits and colimits of presheaves
are formed objectwise.
\end{enumerate}
\end{construction}

\begin{theorem}[Completion and exact recovery of concurrent arrows]
\label{thm:egt-day-preservation}
The category $\widehat{\mathcal C}$ is complete, cocomplete, and
symmetric monoidal closed under the displayed operations. Tensor
preserves colimits separately. Yoneda is fully faithful and strong
symmetric monoidal, and preserves the original internal hom:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
